{"concepts_used":["GC-0036","GC-0001","GC-0002","GC-0038","GC-0168"],"decline_reason":"","declined":false,"citations":[{"ref":"TMA1995/s43","quote":"An application for the registration of a trade mark in respect of particular goods or services must be rejected if, because of some connotation that the trade mark or a sign contained in the trade mark has, the use of the trade mark in relation to those goods or services would be likely to deceive or cause confusion."},{"ref":"TMM/Part29/1/1/2","quote":"If a trade mark contains or consists of word/s which connote a particular plant variety or other plant name, and is applied to plants or plant materials of the same or a closely related genus, it is likely to deceive or cause confusion as to the true nature of those plants or plant materials and a ground for rejection under section 43 of the Act will be appropriate."},{"ref":"TMM/Part32A/2/4/2/4/1","quote":"Therefore, if the trade mark contains or consists of a known variety name, the connotation may be immediate, and deception or confusion is likely if the trade mark is used on a different variety of the same or a closely related genus."},{"ref":"TMM/Part32A/2/4/2/4/1","quote":"However, the examiner needs to consider how the variety name appears within the trade mark as a whole. For example, if the plant name is a dictionary word appearing in a phrase then connotation may not be immediate."}],"answer":"Yes, in principle—but using a plant variety name does not by itself establish that a particular application must be rejected.

**Act:** Section 43 requires rejection where a connotation of the mark, or a sign within it, makes use on the claimed goods or services likely to deceive or cause confusion. [TMA1995/s43]

**Manual practice:** A name connoting a particular plant variety can support a section 43 objection for plants or plant materials of the same or a closely related genus. The more detailed guidance identifies the concern as use on a **different variety** of that genus: a known variety name may immediately connote that variety, making use on another variety likely to deceive or confuse. [TMM/Part29/1/1/2; TMM/Part32A/2/4/2/4/1]

**Important qualification—Manual practice:** The examiner must consider the mark as a whole. For example, a variety name that is also a dictionary word appearing within a phrase may not give rise to an immediate connotation. The assessment is therefore not simply whether the mark includes a variety name. This explains the general examination approach, not the outcome of your particular application. [TMM/Part32A/2/4/2/4/1]"}
